beats.narration_text: Research Computing on Explorer and AICR. Scientific Reproducibility. How to make your computational work redoable, by you in six months or by anyone else, with environments, data layout and records.

shot.visual_intent: Film identity and short teaching description, visible immediately; Liam speaks playlist, title, summary

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. First, a correction. Reproducibility is not a favour you do for other scientists. The first person it helps is you, six months from now, when a reviewer asks for one more plot. This lecture is a toolkit for making your research redoable: the three words people confuse, why the field has a crisis, a checklist, how to record your software, conda environments done properly, data organisation, documentation, and what to do tomorrow morning.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. Version control: software that records every change to your files, so you can go back. A module: a piece of software the cluster team installed, loaded by name and version. Conda: a tool that builds isolated environments of packages. An environment: one named set of software, kept apart from all the others. A README: the plain-text file that explains a folder. And a random seed: the number that makes a random process repeat exactly.

beats.narration_text: Three words people mix up. Reproducibility: someone else takes your same data and your same methods and gets your result. Replicability: a different team collects new data, uses similar methods, and finds a comparable result. Repeatability: you yourself re-run the same methods on the same data six months later and get the identical answer. Today is mostly about the first and the third.

beats.narration_text: Why it matters. In 2016 a Nature survey asked scientists whether they had failed to reproduce an experiment. Most had: in chemistry, roughly nine in ten had failed to reproduce someone else's result; in biology, nearly eight in ten; in physics, medicine and earth science, around two in three. Other studies put numbers on it. In psychology, only thirty-six to forty-seven of a hundred studies replicated. In biomedicine, eleven percent of fifty-three landmark cancer studies. In economics, only forty-nine percent of papers even had enough data and code to try.

beats.narration_text: It bites in the real world: clinical decisions built on results no one can reproduce, policy built on models no one can re-run. And it bites you first. In every project something has to be redone, an analysis, a plot. The more reproducible your workflow, the faster that is, and the faster you publish. The usual culprits are five: methods not documented, data and code not shared, software versions not recorded, results that depend on one machine, and absolute file paths baked into code.

Then five barrier cards land in a row, each a small drawn glyph with a 1–3 word label (no methods · not shared · no versions · one machine · absolute paths), each struck with a grey X as named.

beats.narration_text: The checklist, in three phases. At setup: a Git repository, a consistent folder layout, a documented environment, a README. During the work: commented code, relative paths, random seeds set, every data transformation written down, regular commits. At the end: have someone else run it, ship the environment file and the instructions, share the data and the code, and write down the limitations.

shot.visual_intent: Three columns 'setup · during · completion' with checkbox rows that tick as named (4 · 5 · 5 rows, 1–3 word labels); a progress belt runs under the columns from left to right. Act title top-left.

beats.narration_text: And one principle to carry: FAIR, set out in Scientific Data in 2016. Findable: persistent identifiers and metadata. Accessible: stored in open repositories. Interoperable: standard formats. Reusable: clear licensing and documentation.
beats.motion_claim: Four principles, each landing as one large library icon.

beats.narration_text: Version control gets its own lecture, but the idea in one breath: every change is recorded, you can revert to any earlier version, collaborate without overwriting each other, keep the whole history, and experiment on a branch without breaking the code that works.

beats.narration_text: Record your software. If you load a cluster module, write down the version and when you ran it, in the job script or a README. A job script like this one is already a record: Julia one point ten point four, B W A zero point seven point eighteen, bamtools two point five point two. Change it, and copy the file first, or let Git keep the versions. The team's own module install scripts are public on GitHub, so you can see exactly how a module was built.
beats.motion_claim: The training's own commands and files land in order.

beats.narration_text: And don't load modules in your dot bash R C. That hidden file runs in every shell and every program you open on the cluster. Aliases and colours belong there. Modules don't: they break the self-contained job script, so later you can't tell whether a program came from the script or the shell, and they cause dependency conflicts. Keep software in scripts and READMEs.
beats.motion_claim: The training's own commands and files land in order.

beats.narration_text: Conda builds isolated environments. It works on every platform, handles Python and non-Python packages, keeps each project's dependencies apart, and resolves conflicts. On the cluster: get a compute node, load a miniconda module, create an environment with a Python version, activate it with source activate, install, and deactivate when done.

beats.narration_text: Seven habits. Pin the versions that matter; unpinned, conda takes the latest. Prefer the conda-forge channel, the best maintained. Channel order matters: conda searches top to bottom. Install conda packages first, then pip ones. Export the environment, with from history for a cleaner file. Install everything in one session, because conda resolves conflicts across the whole set at once, and an environment grown over months is the one that won't rebuild. And keep environments small: one per analysis, not one to rule them all.

# channels: conda-forge first, then bioconda, then defaults
# one session, all packages; many small environments

beats.narration_text: Picture the two ways to build one. Added to over months, package by package, the environment collects conflicts, and when you try to recreate it, it won't resolve. Built in one session from one file, it resolves once and rebuilds anywhere.

beats.narration_text: Managing them. List your environments. Create one at a specific path, in your project space. Remove one. Clone one as a backup. Update one from its Y M L file, pruning what the file no longer lists. If solving is slow, install mamba and use it in place of conda. And always use source activate: conda activate needs conda init, which rewrites your dot bash R C and fights with Open OnDemand.

beats.narration_text: The complete workflow starts from a file. One environment dot Y M L names the environment, the channels in order, the pinned Python and packages, and the pip extras last.

props.title: environment.yml
props.code:
name: research_project
channels:
  - conda-forge
  - defaults
dependencies:
  - python=3.10
  - numpy=1.24.3
  - pandas=2.0.2
  - matplotlib=3.7.1
  - jupyter
  - pip:
    - seaborn

beats.narration_text: Data. Three folders: raw, which is original and read-only; processed, cleaned and transformed; and metadata, dictionaries and sample IDs. Each with its own README. Make raw read-only with c h mod five five five, with your professor's agreement, since only the owner can change permissions. And name files to sort themselves: ISO dates, version numbers, lowercase, underscores or hyphens, never spaces.

beats.narration_text: Every data folder needs a README: where the data came from, what each variable means and its range, what processing was done, and what's known to be wrong with it.

# Dataset: Participant Survey Responses
## Source
Collected via Qualtrics, January 2024
## Variables
- subject_id: Unique participant identifier (integer, 1-500)
- age: Participant age in years (integer, 18-65, -99=missing)
## Processing
1. Removed duplicate entries
2. Recoded missing values to -99
## Known Issues
- 15 participants have missing age data

beats.narration_text: The project README: what it is in two sentences, how to install, how to run, where the data is, and the reproduction steps as a numbered list someone can follow without you. Then citation, licence, contact.

props.title: README.md
props.code:
# Project Title
Brief description of the project (2-3 sentences)
## Installation
conda env create -f environment.yml
## Reproducibility
1. Clone repository: git clone https://github.com/user/project.git
2. Create environment: conda env create -f environment.yml
3. Run analysis: python src/main_analysis.py
4. Results appear in results/

## Citation · License · Contact

beats.narration_text: In code, give functions docstrings: what it does, parameters, what it returns. And comment the why, not the what. 'Adjust for one-based indexing in the original dataset' tells a reader something. 'Add one to x' does not.

props.code:
def calculate_mean(data):
    """
    Calculate mean of dataset excluding missing values.

    Parameters: data : array-like
    Returns:    float, the mean value
    """
    data = np.array(data)
    return np.nanmean(data)
# Good: explains reasoning
# Adjust for 1-based indexing in original dataset
x = x + 1

beats.narration_text: Five things to keep, and the exercise. Use version control from day one. Document your environment with conda or pip. Organise files systematically: data, source, results. Write the documentation: README, comments, dictionaries. And test reproducibility by having someone else run your code. The exercise: write an environment dot yml with Python three point ten, numpy, pandas and matplotlib; build it; activate it; install a couple more packages; export the final file. Start the next project this way, document as you go, and share when you can. Perfect reproducibility is hard; any improvement counts.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Reproducible means same data, same methods, and someone else gets your result. Most scientists have failed to reproduce a result, and the first person you help is yourself. At setup: Git, a layout, an environment file, a README; during: relative paths, seeds, commits. Job scripts record module versions, and modules never go in dot bash R C. Conda: pin versions, prefer conda-forge, install in one session, keep environments small, export them, and use source activate. Data: raw read-only, READMEs, dictionaries, three-two-one backups. And comment the why.

Audit it against the reproducibility checklist: version control, environment file, folder layout, README, relative paths, random seeds, data README and dictionary, backups.
